scenes.visual: Title card 'Cells or Serum?' over a transparent GREY water flea beside a test tube. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP. COLOUR MAP (both films): bacteria GOLD dots; removal dial and the letter k TEAL; barrier wall BROWN; macrophages and monocytes PURPLE; neutrophils BLUE; receptor sensor glow WHITE-YELLOW; complement C3b small GREEN tags; C3a and C5a ORANGE sparks; water flea drawn transparent GREY. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: In the first film's model, defenses must remove more than half the bacteria every doubling time. But who does the removing: cells, or something dissolved in the blood?
scenes.visual: Brief replay: the wound box with the TEAL dial and corner factor '2 × (1 − k)'. A question mark splits into two icons: a PURPLE cell and a test tube of pale yellow serum.
scenes.narration: In the first film's model, defenses must remove more than half the bacteria every doubling time. But who does the removing: cells, or something dissolved in the blood?

scenes.tts: In the eighteen eighties and nineties, immunologists argued over exactly this. Elie Metchnikoff, a zoologist, championed the cells. He chose an animal he could see through.
scenes.caption: In the 1880s and 1890s, immunologists argued over exactly this. Elie Metchnikoff, a zoologist, championed the cells. He chose an animal he could see through.
scenes.visual: Two columns headed 'cells' and 'serum'. Name card 'Elie Metchnikoff' slides under 'cells'. A magnifier passes over a transparent GREY flea.
scenes.narration: In the 1880s and 1890s, immunologists argued over exactly this. Elie Metchnikoff, a zoologist, championed the cells. He chose an animal he could see through.

scenes.tts: The water flea Daphnia is small and transparent. Some fleas swallow the needle-shaped spores of a budding yeast with their food. The spores pierce the gut wall into the body cavity.
scenes.visual: Cartoon side view of a GREY transparent Daphnia, gut drawn as a tube. Needle-shaped spores (dark grey) pass along the gut and poke through its wall into the body cavity. Label 'yeast spores'.
scenes.narration: The water flea Daphnia is small and transparent. Some fleas swallow the needle-shaped spores of a budding yeast with their food. The spores pierce the gut wall into the body cavity.

scenes.tts: Suppose the flea's blood cells were passive, or even carried the infection. What would you expect them to do with the spores?
scenes.visual: Round GREY-outlined body-cavity cells drift near the spores. Question card: 'passive cells: what happens to the spores?'
scenes.narration: Suppose the flea's blood cells were passive, or even carried the infection. What would you expect them to do with the spores?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Passive cells should ignore the spores, or spread them. Instead, Metchnikoff saw mobile cells crowd onto the spores, surround them, and engulf them.
scenes.visual: The body-cavity cells, now tinted PURPLE as phagocytes, crawl to the spores, cluster, and wrap membrane around each needle. Inset: one cell enclosing a spore in a bubble.
scenes.narration: Passive cells should ignore the spores, or spread them. Instead, Metchnikoff saw mobile cells crowd onto the spores, surround them, and engulf them.

scenes.tts: The outcome tracked the flea's fate. Where the cells destroyed the spores, the infection stopped. Where spores escaped and grew into budding yeast, the flea died.
scenes.visual: Split screen, two fleas. Left: spores fragmented inside PURPLE cells, flea swimming, label 'cells win: lives'. Right: spores bud into yeast filling the body cavity, flea still, label 'spores win: dies'.
scenes.narration: The outcome tracked the flea's fate. Where the cells destroyed the spores, the infection stopped. Where spores escaped and grew into budding yeast, the flea died.

scenes.tts: His eighteen eighty-four paper made the eating cell, the phagocyte, an active defender. But it did not show that the cells work alone.
scenes.caption: His 1884 paper made the eating cell, the phagocyte, an active defender. But it did not show that the cells work alone.
scenes.visual: Card '1884: phagocytes are an active defense'. Below it a second card in grey: 'not shown: that cells work alone'.
scenes.narration: His 1884 paper made the eating cell, the phagocyte, an active defender. But it did not show that the cells work alone.

scenes.tts: In Paris in the eighteen nineties, Jules Bor-day studied serum, the fluid that remains once blood clots. Serum from an animal immunized against a cholera bacterium killed those bacteria.
scenes.caption: In Paris in the 1890s, Jules Bordet studied serum, the fluid that remains once blood clots. Serum from an animal immunized against a cholera bacterium killed those bacteria.
scenes.visual: Name card 'Jules Bordet, Pasteur Institute' slides under the 'serum' column. Tube 1 labelled 'immune serum' with curved GOLD rods labelled 'Vibrio': the rods fade, tick 'kills'. Small inset: a clotted blood tube, the clear fluid above the clot labelled 'serum'.
scenes.narration: In Paris in the 1890s, Jules Bordet studied serum, the fluid that remains once blood clots. Serum from an animal immunized against a cholera bacterium killed those bacteria.

scenes.tts: Heated to about fifty-five degrees, the immune serum lost its power. Fresh serum from an animal never immunized could not kill the bacteria on its own either.
scenes.caption: Heated to about 55 °C, the immune serum lost its power. Fresh serum from an animal never immunized could not kill the bacteria on its own either.
scenes.visual: Tube 2 'immune serum, heated to about 55 °C' over a small flame: rods stay, cross 'no kill'. Tube 3 'fresh normal serum': rods stay, cross 'no kill'.
scenes.narration: Heated to about 55 °C, the immune serum lost its power. Fresh serum from an animal never immunized could not kill the bacteria on its own either.

scenes.tts: Then Bor-day mixed the heated immune serum with the fresh normal serum. The mixture killed again. So the killing needs two separate parts.
scenes.caption: Then Bordet mixed the heated immune serum with the fresh normal serum. The mixture killed again. So the killing needs two separate parts.
scenes.visual: Tubes 2 and 3 pour into tube 4 'heated immune + fresh normal'; the GOLD rods fade, tick 'kills'. Two blocks appear: 'part 1' and 'part 2'.
scenes.narration: Then Bordet mixed the heated immune serum with the fresh normal serum. The mixture killed again. So the killing needs two separate parts.

scenes.tts: One part survives heat and is raised by immunization. We now call it antibody. The other is destroyed by heat and is present in all fresh serum. We call it complement.
scenes.visual: Block 'part 1' relabels 'antibody: survives heat, raised by immunization'. Block 'part 2' relabels 'complement: destroyed by heat, in all fresh serum', tinted GREEN.
scenes.narration: One part survives heat and is raised by immunization. We now call it antibody. The other is destroyed by heat and is present in all fresh serum. We call it complement.

scenes.tts: So which side was right? Watch a bacterium meet complement. Small green tags, a piece called C three b, coat its surface. A neutrophil grabs the coated bacterium quickly.
scenes.caption: So which side was right? Watch a bacterium meet complement. Small green tags, a piece called C3b, coat its surface. A neutrophil grabs the coated bacterium quickly.
scenes.visual: A GOLD bacterium gains small GREEN tags labelled 'C3b'. A BLUE neutrophil extends arms and engulfs it quickly; an untagged GOLD bacterium beside it is caught more slowly (schematic).
scenes.narration: So which side was right? Watch a bacterium meet complement. Small green tags, a piece called C3b, coat its surface. A neutrophil grabs the coated bacterium quickly.

scenes.tts: Coated microbes are eaten far more readily. In the first film's race, that raises k. The cells eat, and the proteins make the eating faster.
scenes.visual: The first film's TEAL dial returns at the corner and its needle ticks upward; label 'complement coating raises k'. The 'cells' and 'serum' columns slide together.
scenes.narration: Coated microbes are eaten far more readily. In the first film's race, that raises k. The cells eat, and the proteins make the eating faster.

scenes.tts: In nineteen oh eight, Metchnikoff shared the Nobel Prize with Paul Ehrlich, who stressed the defenses in serum. Each side had described part of one system.
scenes.caption: In 1908, Metchnikoff shared the Nobel Prize with Paul Ehrlich, who stressed the defenses in serum. Each side had described part of one system.
scenes.visual: Name cards 'Metchnikoff' and 'Paul Ehrlich' meet under one banner '1908 Nobel Prize, shared'. The two columns merge into one labelled 'one system'.
scenes.narration: In 1908, Metchnikoff shared the Nobel Prize with Paul Ehrlich, who stressed the defenses in serum. Each side had described part of one system.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex, one line only: 'Cells and serum proteins are one system: complement speeds phagocytes.'
